articles.summary: China proposes export controls on 12 solar technologies  Solarbytes
articles.full_text:
Beijing proposed controls on 12 solar technologies, covering perovskite, tandem, TOPCon and HJT processes, with public consultation closing on November 15, 2026.
China's Ministry of Commerce proposed export controls on 12 solar manufacturing technologies on October 16, 2026, citing national security concerns involving aerospace and defence applications. The proposal would prohibit exports of certain thin-wafer, perovskite, tandem-cell and fluidized-bed polysilicon production technologies. Advanced solar cell manufacturing processes, including TOPCon, HJT and XBC, would face restrictions rather than complete bans. Exporters must register certain overseas technology transfers until the revised control catalogue is finalised. Public consultation will close on November 15, 2026. The proposed restrictions could affect solar manufacturing expansion in the United States and India, where manufacturers depend on Chinese equipment and expertise.

articles.title: Japan's Export Growth Hits 16.7% on AI Chip Demand, But Trade Deficit Widens - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Japan's Export Growth Hits 16.7% on AI Chip Demand, But Trade Deficit Widens  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Japan's export growth remained solid in September, extending a more than year-long streak of gains driven by robust global demand for artificial intelligence components and automobiles. However, the positive headline figures masked underlying structural vulnerabilities, as a simultaneous surge in energy import costs widened the nation's trade deficit and highlighted the persistent challenges facing the world's fourth-largest economy.
Semiconductors and Autos Drive Export Engine
Official customs data released on Tuesday showed that the value of Japanese exports rose 16.7 percent year-on-year to 10.97 trillion yen, marking the 13th consecutive month of growth. The expansion was primarily fueled by strong outbound shipments of semiconductors and electronic parts, which are essential for the global build-out of AI hardware infrastructure, alongside resilient demand for Japanese automobiles in key overseas markets.
Japan's entrenched position in the global semiconductor supply chain, particularly in the manufacturing of specialized materials and advanced fabrication equipment, has insulated its export sector from the broader slowdowns seen in consumer electronics. As technology giants in the United States and China continue to invest heavily in data centers and AI processing capabilities, Japanese component manufacturers have reaped the benefits of this structural shift in global capital expenditure.
Energy Costs and the Widening Deficit
Despite the robust export performance, Japan's trade balance slipped further into the red. Imports climbed 18.9 percent year-on-year, driven heavily by a staggering 51.1 percent jump in the value of petroleum imports. As a nation fundamentally lacking in domestic fossil fuel resources, Japan remains acutely vulnerable to global commodity price fluctuations, a vulnerability that is severely magnified by the structural weakness of the yen.
The resulting trade deficit widened to 536.6 billion yen for the month of September, exceeding market expectations and underscoring the heavy toll that a depreciated currency takes on the national balance sheet. While a weaker yen inflates the yen-denominated value of exports and boosts the repatriated earnings of multinational manufacturers, it simultaneously acts as a severe tax on domestic households and small businesses that rely on imported energy and food.
Shifting Bilateral Trade Dynamics
The September data also revealed notable shifts in Japan's bilateral trade relationships. The country maintained a significant trade surplus with the United States, reflecting sustained American consumer demand for Japanese vehicles and machinery. Conversely, Japan continued to run a substantial deficit with China, a reflection of evolving supply chain dynamics and the uneven pace of economic recovery across the Asian continent.
One striking anomaly in the customs data was an 820 percent surge in the value of crude oil imports from the United States. This dramatic pivot away from traditional Middle Eastern suppliers suggests a strategic recalibration by Japanese energy traders, potentially motivated by favorable pricing differentials or long-term energy security agreements negotiated between Tokyo and Washington amid ongoing geopolitical instability in the Gulf.
Macroeconomic Headwinds and Policy Constraints
For the Bank of Japan and the cabinet office, the September trade figures present a complex policy dilemma. The resilience of the manufacturing sector demonstrates that Japanese industry remains globally competitive and capable of capitalizing on the technological revolutions of the 2020s. However, the persistent, structurally driven trade deficits complicate the government's efforts to achieve sustainable, wage-driven domestic inflation.
When import costs consistently outpace export revenues, it drains national income and suppresses real wage growth, making it difficult for policymakers to confidently normalize monetary policy. The government must now balance the interests of its powerful export conglomerates, which benefit from the weak yen, against the mounting political pressure to alleviate the cost-of-living crisis affecting everyday citizens. Until Japan can secure more stable, affordable energy supplies or transition to higher-value export dominance, its trade balance will likely remain a barometer of its broader economic fragility.
Market Expectations and Future Outlook
While a 16.7 percent increase in exports represents undeniable growth, the figure notably missed the market consensus forecast of a 20.1 percent gain. Analysts point to temporary supply chain disruptions and base-effects from the previous year as contributing factors to the relative deceleration. The missed expectations triggered a muted response in Tokyo's equity markets, where investors are increasingly focused on domestic corporate governance reforms rather than macroeconomic trade data.
Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, economists project that Japan's export momentum may face headwinds if global interest rates remain elevated and dampen capital investment in Western markets. Furthermore, any stabilization or strengthening of the yen would immediately compress the profit margins of Japan's automotive and electronics giants. Consequently, the September data serves as a critical baseline, illustrating a manufacturing powerhouse that is currently thriving on the AI boom but remains fundamentally constrained by its resource dependencies and currency dynamics.

articles.title: Japan Posts ¥536.6 Billion September Trade Deficit as Semiconductor Exports Fail to Meet Expectations - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Japan Posts ¥536.6 Billion September Trade Deficit as Semiconductor Exports Fail to Meet Expectations  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Japan's Ministry of Finance on Oct. 21 released preliminary September trade statistics showing exports rose 16.7% year-on-year to ¥10.9723 trillion (approximately $69.4 billion), marking a 13th consecutive month of growth but falling well short of the 20.1% market estimate. Imports climbed 18.9% to ¥11.5088 trillion (approximately $72.8 billion), also below the expected 19.6%. Netting the two out, the September trade balance came to a deficit of ¥536.6 billion (approximately $3.4 billion), not only the fifth consecutive monthly shortfall but also far above the market-expected ¥181 billion (approximately $1.1 billion), widening 93.2% from the ¥277.7 billion (approximately $1.8 billion) deficit in the same month last year.
The data reveal a dual pressure on Japan's trade structure: while semiconductor-related demand is propping up export momentum, it is insufficient to offset swelling import costs for energy and electronic components. The Ministry of Finance noted that September export growth was driven mainly by semiconductor and other electronic components (up 49.4% year-on-year), semiconductor and other manufacturing equipment (up 43.9%) and automobiles (up 15.1), with the export value hitting a record high for the month and the third-highest level for any single month on record. On the import side, crude oil import value soared 51.1%, semiconductor and other electronic component imports jumped 51.4% and liquefied natural gas import value rose 39.2%, pushing total imports to a record high for the month and the second-highest single-month level on record.
By region, Japan's September exports to the United States rose 22.9% year-on-year to ¥1.963 trillion (approximately $12.4 billion), growing for a seventh consecutive month and setting a record high for the month, driven mainly by automobiles, pharmaceuticals and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Imports from the United States surged 44.8% to ¥1.5702 trillion (approximately $9.9 billion). Netting the two out, Japan's trade surplus with the United States shrank 23.4% to ¥392.8 billion (approximately $2.5 billion), contracting for a 10th consecutive month. Notably, the value of Japan's crude oil imports from the United States soared 819.7% and LNG imports jumped 541.6%, reflecting a structural shift in energy procurement sources.
As for China, Japan's September exports to China rose 8.6% year-on-year to ¥1.73 trillion (approximately $10.9 billion), growing for a seventh consecutive month; imports from China jumped 16.4% to ¥2.7572 trillion (approximately $17.4 billion), a record high for the month, bringing the trade deficit with China to ¥1.0272 trillion (approximately $6.5 billion), the 66th consecutive monthly deficit. Exports to the European Union rose 10.5% year-on-year to ¥985.4 billion (approximately $6.2 billion), growing for a 14th consecutive month, but the deficit came to ¥140.9 billion (approximately $890.8 million), the fifth straight monthly shortfall. Exports to Asia excluding China rose 17.5% year-on-year to ¥6.0736 trillion (approximately $38.4 billion), a record high for the month, with imports also hitting a record for the period, causing the surplus to plunge 80.2% to ¥47.1 billion (approximately $297.8 million).
For the first half of fiscal 2026 (April through September), Japan's trade deficit reached ¥2.8184 trillion (approximately $17.8 billion), nearly double the ¥1.2829 trillion (approximately $8.1 billion) deficit in the same period last year, an increase of 98.8%. Exports for the period rose 18.4% year-on-year to ¥63.457 trillion (approximately $401.2 billion), while imports rose 20.4% to ¥66.2754 trillion (approximately $419.0 billion), both setting record highs. The surplus with the United States came to ¥2.1224 trillion (approximately $13.4 billion), down 35.1% from a year earlier, indicating that U.S. tariff and trade policy adjustments continue to weigh on Japan's surplus structure.

Note: Market estimates are the median forecasts of private research institutions.
Regional export performance also showed across-the-board growth:
| Region | Export value | Year-on-year change | Trade balance | 
|---|---|---|---|
| United States | ¥1.963 trillion (approximately $12.4 billion) | +22.9% | Surplus of ¥392.8 billion (approximately $2.5 billion) |

Note: Asia excluding China figures reflect the surplus calculated from separately tallied exports and imports.
The below-expectation export growth partly reflects base effects. The export growth rate stood at 19.3% in August before slowing to 16.7% in September, a marked deceleration; the import growth rate fell from 28.0% in August to 18.9%, indicating that domestic demand-driven purchasing is also cooling.
At the same time, South Korea's exports for the first 20 days of this month more than doubled year-on-year, with semiconductor exports surging more than 2.2-fold to account for nearly 45% of total exports, and chip sales hitting a record high. By comparison, while Japan's semiconductor-related exports maintained high growth, overall export growth still fell short of market expectations, highlighting a divergence in how the two countries are benefiting from the semiconductor cycle.
Financial markets reacted positively to the data. The Nikkei 225 surged 1.80%, or 1,155.59 points, to 65,231.01 in morning trading on Oct. 21; the Japanese yen weakened 0.09% to ¥158.32 per dollar, extending its recent soft trend. While a weaker yen helps export competitiveness, it simultaneously inflates energy and raw material import costs, creating a double-edged sword for the trade balance.
From an industry perspective, the sustained high growth in semiconductor equipment and electronic component exports confirms that global artificial intelligence (AI)-related investment demand remains resilient, while 15.1% growth in auto exports shows that Japanese automakers' sales momentum in the U.S. market has not visibly weakened. However, the simultaneous surge in crude oil and LNG import values makes it difficult to narrow the trade deficit, keeping Japan in a deficit position for five consecutive months.
For investors, the key signal in this data lies in the import structure of "rising volumes and rising prices." Record-high exports alongside a widening deficit mean limited improvement in the terms of trade; if the yen continues to trade weakly around ¥158, import cost pressure will be even harder to alleviate. On the other hand, the 10th consecutive month of contraction in the U.S. surplus and the 35.1% plunge in the first-half U.S. surplus also add variables to Japan's position in U.S. trade negotiations.
Going forward, the focus will be on whether semiconductor exports can sustain high growth, whether energy import prices will retreat, and the seesaw effect of yen exchange rate trends on both exports and imports. Market participants believe that if import growth continues to outpace export growth, Japan's trade balance is unlikely to escape its deficit pattern in the near term.

October 21, 2026 at 17:50 JST
Tokyo Container Terminal is seen in Tokyo on Feb. 19, 2025. (AP file photo)
Japan’s trade deficit reached 2.81 trillion yen ($17.8 billion) for the first fiscal half, according to government data released Wednesday, as the war in Iran sent oil import prices soaring.
The Finance Ministry’s preliminary data showed that Japan’s exports for the April-September period grew 18.4% from the same period the previous year to 63.5 trillion yen, while imports soared to 66.3 trillion yen, up 20.4% year-over-year.
Both were record highs for Japan. The soaring price of oil affects a wide range of sectors, including plastic goods and shipping costs.
Resource-poor Japan imports virtually all its oil and has relied on access to the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East for its oil shipments. That’s now basically blocked, and Japan has had to pay more to get shipments from other routes.
Brent crude, the international standard, has soared from $70 a barrel in February to around $110 a barrel. Analysts say prices are unlikely to ease soon.
For the month of September, Japan’s trade deficit totaled 536.6 billion yen, marking the fifth month of deficits, down from 1.1 trillion yen in August.
Japan’s September imports grew 18.9% from the previous year, while exports rose 16.7%.
One sore point is the weakening yen, which drives up the cost of imports. The U.S. dollar is lately trading at 150-yen levels.
The central bank, which kept borrowing costs at below or near zero for years to help keep a shaky economy going, has been gradually raising interest rates, in part to prop up the yen.
Last month, the Bank of Japan raised the benchmark interest rate to 1.25% from 1.0%, a 31-year high. Its monetary policy board meets again next week. The bank has an inflation target of about 2%.
The Japanese government has repeatedly stressed it’s working closely with the Bank of Japan. The government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is promising a tax cut on food to 1% from 8% to help lower-income families cope with soaring prices. That bill is now being debated in Parliament.

articles.title: Philippines’ trade deficit with China hits $29.13 billion - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: Philippines’ trade deficit with China hits $29.13 billion  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines’ trade deficit with China reached $29.13 billion in 2025, exceeding its combined deficits with its next four largest deficit-generating trading partners and highlighting the country’s heavy reliance on Chinese goods amid continuing maritime tensions in the West Philippine Sea.
According to data from the Philippine Statistics Authority cited in an analysis by Inquirer data scientist Dr. Alicor Panao, the Philippines imported $38.44 billion worth of goods from China last year while exporting only $9.31 billion.
The country’s trade deficits with Indonesia, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam totaled $25.29 billion, still less than its deficit with China alone.
The Philippines recorded deficits of $9.21 billion with Indonesia, $7.30 billion with South Korea, $4.67 billion with Thailand and $4.11 billion with Vietnam.
In contrast, the country maintained a $5.31 billion trade surplus with the United States, its primary diplomatic and security partner, according to the analysis.
The Philippines also recorded trade surpluses of $10.43 billion with Hong Kong, $3.10 billion with the Netherlands, $1.17 billion with Germany and $946 million with Japan.
The surpluses with Hong Kong, the Netherlands, Germany and Japan totaled roughly $15.65 billion, while the combined surpluses with the United States and those four trading partners amounted to approximately $20.96 billion.

However, Panao, an associate professor at the University of the Philippines, noted that these surpluses were insufficient to offset the volume of goods imported from China, including electronic equipment, industrial machinery, iron and steel, and everyday consumer products.
He said the trade figures reflect the Philippine economy’s heavy dependence on Chinese industrial goods and electronic components, partly because the country’s domestic manufacturing capacity in these sectors remains limited.
While maritime incidents in the West Philippine Sea continue to draw international attention, the analysis said the trade relationship represents another important dimension of Philippine-China relations.
“As the Philippines asserts its sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea, the trade data suggests that long-term stability will also require stronger domestic productive capacity,” Panao said.
Panao added: “Alongside a bolder articulation of its territorial rights, maybe it is time for the country to rebuild local industries and diversify its supply chains, so it can gradually build economic resilience and lessen its reliance on any single trading partner.” /dm

articles.full_text:
France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.
With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.
The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.
Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.
Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.
No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.
International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.
Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.
“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

Every morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.
Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.
They’re on their way to work too. But the federal agents who form this second army are on a different mission.
Unlike the builders, they are not forging the US’s future one new starter home at a time. Their job is to pursue those who do the building: they follow the framers, track down the roofers, chase the cement masons and concrete finishers.
They are hunters.
“In Texas, you go deer hunting in the early morning,” said Jacob Monty, an immigration lawyer in Houston. “That’s what they are doing. They are hunting for construction workers, early in the morning, like you would an animal.”
Texas and its construction workforce are the ground zero of Donald Trump’s latest mass deportation effort, dubbed ICE 2.0. As the US president has pivoted from last year’s militarized “invasions” of Los Angeles and Minneapolis to this year’s less visible but no less devastating stop-and-search tactics, he has found rich pickings in Texas.
Texas is seeing by far the greatest number of ICE arrests in the country. More than 12,000 in July alone, almost double the number in the next most affected states, Florida and California.
Many of the detainees are Hispanic builders. Of every 10 construction workers in Texas, four are foreign born, most of whom are Hispanic and undocumented.
“This is low-hanging fruit,” Monty said. “If you target Texas Hispanics in trucks, you have a good chance of nabbing an undocumented person, and feeding the mass deportation machine.”
But there is a price to pay for ICE casting its dragnet through Texas barrios and building sites as it seeks to meet its new target of 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The street-level apprehensions are roiling the state, distorting its economy, forcing up house prices and the cost of groceries.
Hispanic families are also being torn apart. Hardworking people are being pushed into the shadows, others disappearing as they flee the country or are deported. The foundations of new homes are lying unfinished, building sites empty.
With the midterm elections just days away, and hugely consequential congressional races as well as the gubernatorial contest hanging in the balance, there are also political costs. Trump appears to be digging a hole for himself with Texas’s Hispanic voters.
Latino Texans who were born in the US or have naturalised, and thus can vote, are increasingly angry and confused. Many of them voted for Trump two years ago, attracted by his promise of a stronger economy and a fortified border that would keep out “criminal” immigrants.
They delivered Trump a historic victory, even in majority-Hispanic districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century – voters like Sergio Benavides, 44, the owner of a home-building construction company in the Texas borderlands of the Rio Grande valley.
A naturalised US citizen, he voted for Trump in 2024. He liked his campaign promises that he would lower prices and secure the border. When people warned him it would turn sour, he didn’t listen.
He’s listening now. The prices of homes, food and gas have all gone up. Workers have to be paid more because so many have been deported. One of his subcontractors and his wife have disappeared, picked up by ICE, leaving behind three US-citizen children.
“That makes me sad,” he said. “We are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and grow. This is not what I thought when I voted for Trump.”
Benavides is part of a backlash that is showing up in the polls. Latino voters are turning against the president on the very issues that drew them to him – the cost of living, and immigration enforcement.
A poll last month from Equis Research found that disapproval of Trump had risen to 63% among Texas Latinos. In the critical US Senate race, which could determine which party holds the upper chamber during Trump’s final two years in office, 58% of likely Latino voters intend to back the Democratic candidate James Talarico, while only 33% support the scandal-ridden Republican, Ken Paxton. This, in a state that last returned a Democrat to the US Senate in 1988.
Latinos make up a third of Texas’s registered voters, the second-highest number in the country. And they know it.
Construction workers among them.
Marco Antonio Osorio’s day begins at 5am. Same routine, six days a week.
A member of his crew comes to pick him up at his house in Houston. They drive around in their shared white truck gathering other crew, then head off to the site of a new apartment complex where they spend the next 10 hours laying TV and wifi fiber optic cables.
It’s their speciality. They are good at it, and in demand. If only they were left to get on with it.
Around the beginning of the year Osorio, 50, noticed a surge in ICE street activity. “There were so many more sheriff’s vehicles, state troopers, ICE on the highways weaving between cars checking plates.”
As an undocumented Mexican who came to the US in 1993, aged 17, he knew he was vulnerable. But he thought he had some cover. His US-born daughter Gabriela is serving as a marine at Camp Pendleton in California. She has helped him apply for residency, and the paperwork is being processed.
Still, he wasn’t taking chances. He changed his habits. No going out of the house unless for essentials. No nights out at the movies. He couldn’t stop working, or else how would he pay the bills? But now he wears a button-down shirt on the drive to the site rather than his fluorescent yellow vest. No point advertising himself as a construction worker with ICE on the hunt.
He told his company he didn’t want to work outside Houston any more. The freeways to Austin and San Antonio were crawling with cop cars. “The company told me there weren’t any jobs here – either go out of town, or you don’t work.”
So he took a job in Austin. On 10 June, as he was returning home after another 10-hour shift, a sheriff’s car did a U-turn on the freeway and pulled him over. The officer said it was because his truck had a faulty rear light, but Osorio asked himself how they could have known that as they were traveling in opposite directions. More likely, he thought, was that his vehicle has a clear front screen. “They could see we were Hispanic.”
Within two minutes of the traffic stop, ICE SUVs blocked him in, front and back. The speed with which they appeared, Osorio realised, meant it had to be coordinated.
He told them his daughter was a US marine. He showed the officers the receipt for his residency application. An ICE officer replied: “Oh, that doesn’t count.” They took him to a freezing cell, the notorious las hieleras, and from there to an immigration detention facility near the border. He spent 40 days in the wilderness of ICE custody, until Monty got him released for lack of due process.
As he awaits his appeal, Osorio continues to work. Those bills keep coming, his children need feeding. On drives to work sites in Houston, he thinks about his daughter serving the country whose government wants him gone. He worries about his youngest child, an autistic boy, and what will become of him. He imagines returning to Mexico, a place he hasn’t known for 33 years.
As he drives, he spots apartment blocks all over the city that he helped put up. And he’s proud. “See those – I worked there 10 years ago. Or those – we built them 15 years ago.”
He thinks to himself: “This is my home.”
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a Mexican national, had been in the US for 35 years, two longer than Osorio. A house framer, the skilled worker who puts up the wooden skeleton of new houses, he carried out his days with an identical drill. Out the door at 5am, pick up the crew, 10 hours of hard graft, then relax on the balcony of his self-built Houston home listening to tierra caliente music with Ñoño, his beloved dog whom he named after a podgy 1970s Mexican sitcom character.
When ICE began to crank up its street arrests in February, Salgado spotted an opportunity. Many workers were too scared to leave the house, and new homes were standing half finished. A fearless entrepreneur, Salgado began accepting jobs that other undocumented framers like him would not contemplate.
He took precautions. He swapped his construction vest for a suit jacket while driving to work. He removed the jumble of blueprints, invoices and receipts from the dashboard of his white van. It was like his mobile office on wheels, but it branded him as a building professional, so he cleaned it off.
As time passed, and the ICE presence grew more oppressive, his three sons grew concerned. They are all American-born US citizens, and Salgado had high aspirations for them. They weren’t going to be builders like him – they were going to be educated, fulfill their own American dream. Ronaldo Salgado, the eldest, is a history teacher; Lorenzo Salgado Jr studied at the prestigious Tufts University and is now an engineer in Washington DC; and the youngest is at college, also studying engineering.
The sons got together and prepared a plan for their dad. They gave him a phone number that he should call if ever he were stopped, and they made sure he carried a “know your rights” card in his wallet. They made him swear that he would never sign any ICE form, as they feared he would be hoodwinked into self-deporting.

The Department of Commerce will submit the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and clearance in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, on or after the date of publication of this notice. We invite the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. Public comments were previously requested via the
Federal Register
on June 3, 2026, during a 60-day comment period. This notice allows for an additional 30 days for public comments.
Agency:
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Commerce.
Title:
The Ocean Enterprise: A study of US business activity in ocean measurement, observation and forecasting.
OMB Control Number:
0648-0712.
Form Number(s):
None.
Type of Request:
Regular submission. Extension of approved collection.
Number of Respondents:
250.
Average Hours per Response:
0.40 (24 minutes).
Total Annual Burden Hours:
100.
Needs and Uses:
This is a request for extension of an approved information collection. NOAA's National Ocean Service's U.S. Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS) Office is requesting approval to continue a web-based survey of employers who provide either services or infrastructure to IOOS or organizations that add value to the IOOS data and other outputs by tailoring them for specific end uses. The purpose of the survey and overall project is to gather information to
( printed page 66549)
articulate the collective and derived value of the IOOS enterprise and to create a profile of businesses and organizations who are involved with providing services or utilizing IOOS data for other specific end uses. This survey was conducted in FY2015, FY2020, and FY2025 and is intended to be repeated on a regular basis in order to track the growth of the U.S. Ocean Enterprise. The survey provides critical assessment data and is necessary in order to collect demographic, financial, and functional information for each organization with regard to their involvement with IOOS. Data from this web survey will be analyzed and used to produce a final report. The results will demonstrate the size and economic impact of IOOS data to the United States marine ocean sector.
Affected Public:
Business or other for-profit organizations and Not-for-profit institutions.
Frequency:
Once every 5 years.
Respondent's Obligation:
Voluntary.
Legal Authority:
Section 12304 of the Integrated Coastal and Ocean Observation System Act, part of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (Pub. L. 111-11), and reauthorized under the Coordinated Ocean Observations and Research Act of 2020 (Pub. L. 116-271).
This information collection request may be viewed at
www.reginfo.gov. Follow the instructions to view the Department of Commerce collections currently under review by OMB.
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of this notice on the following website:
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain. Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function and entering either the title of the collection or the OMB Control Number 0648-0712.

Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

AGENCY:
Office of the Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or the Department) is notifying the public that there will be no Civil Monetary Penalty (CMP) inflation adjustment for 2026 in accordance with the April 17, 2026, guidance from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). HHS
( printed page 66567)
will continue to use the 2025 civil monetary penalty levels because there will be no cost-of-living adjustment for 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jennifer Johnson, Deputy Assistant Secretary, Office of Acquisitions, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources, Room 536-H, Hubert Humphrey Building, 200 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20201; (771) 215-0133.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015 (section 701 of Pub. L. 114-74) amended the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act of 1990 (Pub. L. 101-410, 104 Stat. 890 (1990)), which is intended to improve the effectiveness of CMPs and to maintain the deterrent effect of such penalties requires agencies to adjust the CMPs for inflation annually.
HHS lists the CMP authorities and the amounts administered by its Divisions in tabular form in 45 CFR 102.3, which was issued in an interim final rule published in the September 6, 2016,
Federal Register
(81 FR 61538). Annual adjustments were subsequently published on February 3, 2017 (82 FR 9175), October 11, 2018 (83 FR 51369), November 5, 2019 (84 FR 59549), January 17, 2020 (85 FR 2869), November 15, 2021 (86 FR 62928), March 17, 2022 (87 FR 15100), October 6, 2023 (88 FR 69531), August 8, 2024 (89 FR 64815), and January 28, 2026 (91 FR 3665).
II. Calculation of 2025 Fiscal Year Penalties
The annual inflation adjustment for each applicable CMP is determined using the percent increase in the Consumer Price Index for all Urban Consumers (CPI-U) for the month of October of the year in which the amount of each CMP was most recently established or modified. In the December 17, 2024, OMB Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, M-25-02, “Implementation of Penalty Inflation Adjustments for 2025, Pursuant to the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015,” OMB published the multiplier for the required annual adjustment. The cost-of-living adjustment multiplier for 2025, based on the CPI-U for the month of October 2024, not seasonally adjusted, was 1.02598. The multiplier was applied to each applicable penalty amount that was updated and published for fiscal year 2024 and was rounded to the nearest dollar. Those CMP updates were published at 91 FR 3665.
III. Cancellation of 2026 Penalty Inflation Adjustment
Due to a lapse in appropriations from October 1, 2025, until November 12, 2025, BLS was unable to produce the October 2025 CPI-U data. As a result, there was no inflation adjustment multiplier for 2026, which is needed to adjust civil monetary penalties for the 2026 calendar year under the 2015 Act. On April 17, 2026, OMB issued Memorandum M-26-11 informing agencies of the cancellation of the inflation adjustment for 2026. As a result, HHS will continue using the maximum civil monetary penalties as adjusted for inflation by the 2025 adjustment for all penalties imposed after January 15, 2025.
Gustav Chiarello,
Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources, Department of Health and Human Services.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Assistant Regional Administrator for Sustainable Fisheries, Greater Atlantic Region, NMFS, has made a preliminary determination that an Exempted Fishing Permit (EFP) application contains all of the required information and warrants further consideration. The EFP would allow federally permitted fishing vessels to fish outside fishery regulations in support of exempted fishing activities proposed by the Maine Department of Marine Resources (ME DMR). Regulations under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act require publication of this notification to provide interested parties the opportunity to comment on applications for proposed EFPs.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before November 5, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit written comments by email:
nmfs.gar.efp@noaa.gov.
Include in the subject line “ME DMR Ventless Trap EFP.” All comments received are a part of the public record and may be posted for public viewing without change. All personal identifying information (
e.g.,
name, address), confidential business information, or otherwise sensitive information submitted voluntarily by the sender will be publicly accessible. NMFS will accept anonymous comments (enter “anonymous” as the signature if you wish to remain anonymous).
The applicant submitted a complete application for an EFP to conduct commercial fishing activities that the regulations would otherwise restrict. This EFP would exempt the participating vessels from the following Federal regulations:
To allow for closed escape vents and smaller trap mesh and entrance heads.
§ 697.19(a)-(e)
Trap limit requirements
To allow for 3 additional traps per fishing vessel, for a total of up to 60 additional traps.
§ 697.19(j)
Trap tag requirements
To allow for the use of untagged traps (though each modified trap will have the participating fisherman's identification attached).
§§ 697.20(a), 697.20(d), 697.20(g), and 697.20(h)(1) and (2)
Possession restrictions
To allow for onboard biological sampling of undersized, v-notched, and egg-bearing American lobsters and undersized and egg-bearing Jonah crabs.
Table 2—Project Summary
Project title
Maine lobster fishery-dependent offshore ventless and commercial trap research program.
Project start
1/01/2027.
Project end
12/31/2027.
Project objectives
To conduct a survey, in partnership with the Commercial Fisheries Research Foundation (CFRF), to provide distribution, abundance, and biological data on juvenile lobsters and Jonah crabs from times and areas in Federal waters of the Gulf of Maine with low coverage from traditional surveys.
Project location
Gulf of Maine: Statistical Areas 511, 512, and 513.
Number of vessels
Up to 20.
Number of trips
Up to 36 per vessel; up to 720 total.
Trip duration (days)
Up to 3 days.
Total number of days
Up to 108 per vessel; up to 2,160 total.
Gear type(s)
Trap.
Number of tows or sets
1 per trip; up to 720 total.
Duration of tows or sets
7-10 days.
Project Narrative
This EFP would contribute to the ongoing effort by the ME DMR and CFRF to collect data on juvenile lobster and Jonah crab abundance and distribution in areas and times of the year with low or no coverage by traditional surveys. The study is designed to inform management by addressing questions about changing reproduction and recruitment dynamics of lobster and to develop a foundation of knowledge for the data-deficient Jonah crab fishery. This would be year 4 of an ongoing project.
The 2025 survey included 18 harvesters participating in the program; and in 2026, 16 harvesters participated in the program. There are currently 33 ventless traps deployed within Lobster Management Area 1, spanning Statistical Areas 511, 512, and 513. As of September 8, 2026, there have been 807 sampling events from ventless traps, with a total of 10,497 biological samples from lobsters and crabs recorded.
Year 4 of this project would continue the program using up to 20 federally permitted Maine lobster vessels. Each vessel would fish with 3 modified, ventless traps designed to catch juvenile lobsters, totaling up to 60 modified traps. The ventless trap configuration is as follows: 40-inch (101.6-centimeter) length x 21-inch (53.34-centimeter) width x 14-inch (35.56-centimeter) height, single parlor, 1-inch (2.54-centimeter) square rubber-coated 12-gauge (2.05-millimeter) wire, standard shrimp mesh netting, cement runners,
( printed page 66548)
and 4-inch (10.16-centimeter) x 6-inch (15.24-centimeter) disabling door. The modified traps would adhere to the standard coastwide survey gear for lobster and Jonah crab set by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) and would be fished with standard Atlantic Large Whale Take Reduction Plan-compliant trawls.
The study would take place during regular fishing activity of the participating vessels but catch from the modified traps would remain separate from that of standard gear. Operators would collect data on size, sex, presence of eggs, and shell hardness for lobsters and Jonah crabs, and v-notch and shell disease for lobsters. Operators would return all specimens from modified gear to the ocean once sampling is complete.
All data collected by the participants using the CFRF data collection app would be sent to ME DMR for processing. ME DMR would then share final datasets with CFRF, to further share with the Atlantic Coastal Cooperative Statistics Program, the Northeast Fisheries Science Center, and the ASMFC.
If approved, the applicant may request minor modifications and extensions to the EFP throughout the year. EFP modifications and extensions may be granted without further notice if they are deemed essential to facilitate completion of the proposed research and have minimal impacts that do not change the scope or impact of the initially approved EFP request. Any fishing activity conducted outside the scope of the exempted fishing activity would be prohibited.

Organization and Structure of the Application/Annual Report Guidance.

AGENCY:
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
                    ACTION:
Notice and request for comments.
                    SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, FMCSA announces its plan to submit the Information Collection Request (ICR) described below to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval and invites public comment. FMCSA requests approval to renew an ICR titled, “Training Certification for Entry-Level Commercial Motor Vehicle Operators,” which will continue to be used to register providers of entry-level driver training and to provide State Drivers' Licensing Agencies with information on individuals who have completed said training. If approved, this renewal will allow FMCSA to continue to collect information on registered training providers and entry-level driver training certification information until 2030.
                    DATES:
Comments on this notice must be received on or before December 21, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by Docket Number FMCSA-2026-3334 using any of the following methods:
- Federal eRulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
                    
- Mail:
                         Dockets Operations; U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
                    
- Hand Delivery or Courier:
                         Dockets Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001 between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
                    
- Fax:
                         (202) 493-2251.
                    
                        To avoid duplication, please use only one of these four methods. See the “Public Participation and Request for Comments” portion of the 
                        SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
                         section for instructions on submitting comments.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Instructions
                    All submissions must include the Agency name and docket number. For detailed instructions on submitting comments, see the Public Participation heading below. Note that all comments received will be posted without change to 
                    https://www.regulations.gov, including any personal information provided. Please see the Privacy Act heading below.
                
Public Participation and Request for Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this notice (FMCSA-2026-3334), indicate the specific section of this document to which your comment applies, and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and a mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so FMCSA can contact you if there are questions regarding your submission.
                    To submit your comment online, go to 
                    https://www.regulations.gov/docket/FMCSA-2026-3334/document, click on this notice, click “Comment,” and type your comment into the text box on the following screen.
                
                    If you submit your comments by mail or hand delivery, submit them in an unbound format, no larger than 8
                    1/2
                     by 11 inches, suitable for copying and electronic filing.
                
FMCSA will consider all comments and material received during the comment period.
Privacy Act
                    In accordance with 5 U.S.C. 553(c), DOT solicits comments from the public to better inform its regulatory process. DOT posts these comments, including any personal information the commenter provides, to 
                    www.regulations.gov
                     as described in the system of records notice DOT/ALL 14 (Federal Docket Management System (FDMS)), which can be reviewed at 
                    https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/privacy/privacy-act-system-records-notices. The comments are posted without edits and are searchable by the name of the submitter.
                
Background
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety regulations require minimum training standards for entry-level drivers, and include two separate information collection actions: (1) Training providers must electronically submit information to FMCSA's Training Provider Registry (TPR) to ensure that they meet the new training provider eligibility requirements and may therefore be listed on a new TPR; and (2) after an individual driver-trainee completes training administered by a training provider listed on the TPR, that training provider must electronically submit training certification information regarding the driver-trainee to the TPR. While there have been a number of regulatory actions delaying compliance with these requirements, all have been in effect since February 7, 2022. The information collection estimates included in this renewal action are based on actual data from the TPR and from training certification transactions over the past year.
                    Title:
                     Training Certification for Entry-Level Commercial Motor Vehicle Operators.
                
                    OMB Control Number:
                     2126-0028.
                
                    Type of Request:
                     Renewal of a currently-approved ICR.
                
                    Respondents:
                     Training Providers.
                
                    Estimated Number of Respondents:
                     26,284.
                
                    Estimated Time per Response:
                     0.55 hours.
                
                    Expiration Date:
                     February 28, 2027.
                
                    Frequency of Response:
                     All training providers will need to initially register once. Additionally, all registered training providers must update their information at least biennially. They are also required to provide an update if any key information (company name, address, phone number, types of training offered, etc.) changes prior to their biennial update. After an individual driver-trainee completes training administered by a training provider listed on the TPR, that training provider must submit training certification information regarding the driver-trainee to the TPR.
                
                    Estimated Total Annual Burden:
                     198,730 hours.
                
                    Public Comments Invited:
                     You are asked to comment on any aspect of this information collection, including: (1) whether the proposed collection is necessary for the performance of FMCSA's functions; (2) the accuracy of the estimated burden; (3) ways for FMCSA to enhance the quality, usefulness, and clarity of the collected information; and (4) ways that the burden could be minimized without reducing the quality of the collected information. The Agency will summarize or include your comments in the request for OMB's clearance of this ICR.
                
                    Issued under the authority of 49 CFR 1.87.
Jonathan Mueller,
Acting Associate Administrator, Office of Research and Registration.

The following Grant Guideline is adopted by the State Justice Institute for FY 2027.

I. Eligibility
Pursuant to the State Justice Institute Act of 1984 (42 U.S.C. 10701et seq.), the State Justice Institute (SJI) is authorized to award grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts to State and local courts, national nonprofit organizations, and others for the purpose of improving the quality of justice in the State courts of the United States.
SJI is authorized by Congress to award grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts to the following entities and types of organizations:
National nonprofit organizations controlled by, operating in conjunction with, and serving the judicial branches of State governments (42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(1)(B)).
National nonprofit organizations for the education and training of judges and support personnel of the judicial branch of State governments (42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(1)(C)). An applicant is considered a national education and training applicant under section 10705(b)(1)(C) if:
the principal purpose or activity of the applicant is to provide education and training to State and local judges and court personnel, and
the applicant demonstrates a record of substantial experience in the field of judicial education and training.
Other eligible grant recipients (42 U.S.C. 10705 (b)(2)(A) through (D)).
Provided that the objectives of the project can be served better, SJI is also authorized to make awards to:
nonprofit organizations with expertise in judicial administration;
institutions of higher education;
individuals, partnerships, firms, and corporations (for-profit organizations must waive their fees); and
private agencies with expertise in judicial administration.
SJI may also make awards to State or local agencies and institutions other than courts for services that cannot be adequately provided through nongovernmental arrangements (42 U.S.C. 10705(b)(3)).
SJI is prohibited from awarding grants to Federal, tribal, and international courts.

foster coordination and cooperation with the Federal judiciary,
promote recognition of the importance of the separation-of-powers

encourage education for judges and support personnel of State court systems through national and State organizations.

SUMMARY:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will submit the information collection abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget for review and clearance in accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. FEMA invites the general public to take this opportunity to comment on a revision of a currently approved information collection. In accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice seeks comments concerning the Community Disaster Loan (CDL) Program. This collection allows the Federal Government to make loans to local governments that have suffered economic problems due to disasters.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 20, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain. Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information or copies of the information collection should be made to Director, Information Management Division, 500 C Street SW, Washington, DC 20472, email address
FEMA-Information-Collections-Management@fema.dhs.gov
or Martha Castro, Section Chief, Program Support and Monitoring Branch, Public Assistance Division, 202-701-4023, or
Martha.Castro@fema.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The information collection is required for Community Disaster Loan (CDL) Program eligibility determinations, CDL management, and compliance with other Federal laws and regulations. The CDL Program is authorized by Section 417 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, Public Law 93-288, as amended, 88 Stat. 143 (42 U.S.C. 5184) and implementing regulations at 44 CFR part 206, subpart K. FEMA may make a CDL to any local government which has suffered a substantial loss of tax or other revenues as a result of a major disaster or emergency and which demonstrates a need for Federal financial assistance to perform its governmental functions.
The CDL must be justified on the basis of need and be based on the actual and projected expenses, as a result of the disaster, for the fiscal year in which the disaster occurred and the three succeeding fiscal years. FEMA has the authority to cancel repayment of all or part of these CDLs to the extent that a determination is made that revenues of the local government during the three fiscal years following the disaster are insufficient to meet the operating budget of that local government because of disaster related revenue losses and additional unreimbursed disaster-related municipal operating expenses.
This proposed information collection previously published in the
Federal Register
on August 4, 2026, at 91 FR 49435 with a 60-day public comment period. FEMA received one comment. The commenter expressed concern about the removal of Part III the Community Disaster Loan Promissory Note, asserting its practical utility for maintaining reliable cash-flow projections for Federal direct loans. FEMA is replacing the speculative, nonbinding projected disbursement schedule with a practical, real-time assessment of actual financial need at the time each loan draw is requested. This updated process prevents local governments from incurring unnecessary interest expenses by ensuring funds are borrowed only when current revenues cannot meet operating obligations. Additionally, this change strengthens the stewardship of Federal funds and improves administrative utility without impacting required credit-subsidy cash-flow forecasting or changing the information collection burden. The purpose of this notice is to notify the public that FEMA will submit the information collection abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget for review and clearance. This 30-day notice updates the type of information collection that was previously published in the 60-day notice as Extension, with a minor change to Revision of a currently approved information collection.

Title:
Application for Community Disaster Loan (CDL) Program.
Type of Information Collection:

1660-0083.

Abstract:
The loan package for the CDL Program provides local governments that have suffered substantial loss of tax or other revenues as a result of a major disaster, the opportunity to obtain financial assistance in order to perform their governmental functions. The loan must be justified on the basis of need and disaster-related expenses.

                    Notice is hereby given that, pursuant to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501 
                    et seq.), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or “Commission”) is submitting to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) this request for extension of the proposed collection of information described below.
                
                    Form N-2 (17 CFR 239.14 and 274.11a-1) is the form used by closed-end management investment companies (“registered closed-end funds”) to register under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-1 
                    et seq.) (“Investment Company Act”), and to register their securities under the Securities Act of 1933 (15 U.S.C. 77a 
                    et seq.) (“Securities Act”). Form N-2 is also used by business development companies (“BDCs”), which are closed-end management investment companies that do not register under the Investment Company Act (but instead elect to be subject to certain provisions of the Investment Company Act (15 U.S.C. 80a-2(a)(48)) to register and offer their securities under the Securities Act.
                
Section 5 of the Securities Act (15 U.S.C. 77e) requires the filing of a registration statement prior to the offer of securities to the public and that the statement be effective before any securities are sold. The primary purpose of the registration process is to provide disclosure of financial and other information to current and potential investors for the purpose of evaluating an investment in a security. Section 5(b) of the Securities Act requires that investors be provided with a prospectus containing the information required in a registration statement prior to the sale, or at the time of confirmation or delivery, of the securities. A closed-end management investment company (that is not a BDC) is required to register as an investment company under Section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act (15 U.S.C. 80a-8(a)). Form N-2 permits a registered closed end fund and a BDC to provide investors with a prospectus covering essential information about the fund when the fund makes an initial or additional offering of its securities. More-detailed information is available to interested investors in the Statement of Additional Information, which is provided to investors upon request and without charge.
The purpose of Form N-2 is to meet the filing and disclosure requirements of the Securities Act and the Investment Company Act and to enable funds to provide investors with information necessary to evaluate an investment in a registered closed-end fund or BDC. The information filed with the Commission permits the verification of compliance with securities law requirements and assures the public availability and dissemination of the information. A registered closed-end fund or BDC must file a registration statement on Form N-2 only when making initial or additional offerings of securities under the Securities Act, or when amending its registration statement. Compliance with the disclosure requirements of Form N-2 is mandatory. Responses to the disclosure requirements will not be kept confidential.
We estimate that approximately 427 respondents file Form N-2 annually, with 1 response annually per respondent at 344 hours per response, including the time and the cost of preparing and reviewing disclosure, filing documents, and retaining records, for a total annual time burden of 146,888 hours. In addition, we estimate the total annual external cost burden associated with Form N-2 to be $9,914,940, based on 30 hours of outside services at a wage rate of $774 per hour for an attorney in the securities industry ($23,220 per response times 427 respondents).
An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB Control Number.

The purpose of the matching program is to identify beneficiaries enrolled in both Medicare and VHA health care and to identify medical claims for which both agencies made payment for the same health care services. The exemption will enable covered drivers to respond to unplanned events that occur outside of, or extend beyond, their normal work hours. Title III of the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 (44 U.S.C. 3583) mandates that the Director of OMB establish a standard application process (SAP) for requesting access to certain confidential data assets. The SAP Portal is a single web-based common application designed to collect information from individuals requesting access to confidential data assets from federal statistical agencies/units.

With the Interagency Council on Statistical Policy (ICSP) as advisors, the entities upon whom this requirement is levied are working with the SAP Project Management Office (PMO) and with OMB to implement the SAP.
The SAP Portal is a single web-based common application designed to collect information from individuals requesting access to confidential data assets from federal statistical agencies and units. When an application for confidential data is approved through the SAP Portal, SAMHSA will collect information to fulfill its data security requirements. This is a required step before providing the individual with access to restricted use microdata for the purpose of evidence building. Agency:
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
Title:
International Dolphin Conservation Program.
OMB Control Number:
0648-0387.

Regular submission [revision and extension of a current information collection].
Number of Respondents:
223 respondents.
Average Hours per Response:
Transit Waiver: 30 minutes, Vessel Permit Application: 35 minutes, Vessel Operator Permit Application: 10 minutes, Vessel Departure Notification: 10 minutes, Permit Operator Notification Changes: 10 minutes, Modified Net Notification: 10 minutes, Experimental Fishing Permit Applications and Reports: 10 hours, Dolphin Mortality Limit Request: 30 minutes, Vessel Register Annual Notification: 33 minutes, Notification Prior to Transfer of Vessel to Foreign Registry and Flag: 5 minutes, Documentary Evidence Requests by Administrator: 30 minutes, Notification of Purse Seine Closure Period: 12 minutes, Force Majeure Exemption Request: 1 hour, Application for IMO number and Exemption Application: 30 minutes, Sunk Status Request: 5 minutes, and Aging Fleet Request: 10 minutes.
Total Annual Burden Hours:
111 hours.
Needs and Uses:
This request is for the revision and extension of OMB Control Number: 0648-0387, sponsored by NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) West Coast Region (WCR). This collection is being revised to remove five (5) of the twenty-one (21) information collections under OMB Control Number: 0648-0387 that were recently added to Control Number 0648-0335, which is sponsored by the NMFS Office of International Affairs, Trade, and Commerce (IATC). The purpose of this revision is to more accurately reflect how the information is being managed. The remaining sixteen (16) information collections are being renewed without modification.
The sixteen unmodified collections of information comply with the requirements of the International Dolphin Conservation Program Act (IDCPA), 16 U.S.C. 1414. The IDCPA amended the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), 16 U.S.C. Ch. 31, and the Dolphin Protection Consumer Information Act (DPCIA), 16 U.S.C. 1385. The IDCPA and the DPCIA authorize the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations that,
inter alia,
implement the dolphin-safe labeling standard in the United States by the collection of documents on the dolphin-safe status of tuna import shipments and domestic tuna product processing; by allowing documentary requests to allow for an effective tracking and verification program; and by verifying that tuna was not harvested by a nation under embargo or otherwise prohibited from exporting tuna to the United States.
The IDCPA allows entry of yellowfin tuna into the United States, under specific conditions, from nations in the International Dolphin Conservation Program that would otherwise be under embargo. The IDCPA also allows U.S. fishing vessels to participate in the yellowfin tuna fishery in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean (ETP) on terms equivalent with the vessels of other nations. NOAA collects information to verify these conditions are met and that allows tracking and verification of “dolphin-safe” and “non-dolphin safe” tuna products from catch through the U.S. market.
This collection of information also complies with the requirements of the Tuna Conventions Act (TCA), 16 U.S.C. 951et seq.,
which was amended by the “Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated Fishing Enforcement Act of 2015” (Pub. L. 114-81). The TCA gives the Secretary of Commerce the authority to enact regulations to fulfill the requirement that all member States maintain and provide to the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC) a list of vessels flagged by the member State and (1) authorized by the member State to be used for fishing for tuna and tuna-like species in the IATTC Convention Area, or (2) authorized by other States to be used for fishing for tuna and tuna-like species in their areas of jurisdiction in the IATTC Area, and to maintain and provide for each vessel on that list certain information on its characteristics and its owner and operator. The TCA also gives the Secretary of Commerce authority to implement fishery management resolutions of the IATTC.
The information is used by NMFS, the United States Coast Guard (USGC), and the IATTC to monitor the size and composition of the vessel fleets in the IATTC Convention Area for compliance and scientific-related purposes. Knowing such information as the number of vessels, the details of the vessels and their ownership, and the types of gear employed enables effective monitoring of vessel activity for enforcement and assessment purposes. NMFS also uses this information for the purposes of managing the U.S. purse seine fleet capacity in the IATTC Convention Area.
This collection includes permit applications, notifications, reports, and certifications that provide information on vessel characteristics and operations in the ETP, documentary evidence requests, and certain other information necessary to implement the IDCPA.
The five information collections being removed from 0648-0387 that were added to 0648-0335 “Tuna Tracking and Verification Program” (90 FR 21752, May 21, 2025), also comply with requirements of the IDCPA and DPCIA. They include vessel arrival notifications, tuna tracking forms, tuna product receiving and processing reports, and documents/certifications that provide information on vessel characteristics and operations in the ETP, the origin of tuna and tuna products, and chain of custody recordkeeping requirements.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of intent to establish a Federal Advisory Committee.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC or Commission) is publishing this notice to announce the intent to establish of 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Federal Advisory Committee (FAC). The Commission has determined that establishing the Committee is necessary and in the public interest.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brian Marenco, Designated Federal Officer, Federal Communications Commission, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, (202) 418-0838, or email:
Brian.Marenco@fcc.gov;
or Logan Bennett, Deputy Designated Federal Officer, Federal Communications Commission, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, (202) 418-7790 or email:
Logan.Bennett@fcc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with section 9(a)(2) of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), 5 U.S.C. 1008, and 41 CFR 102-3.60(a), 102-3.65, and 102-3.35, the Commission is announcing the intent to establish the 4.9 GHz Band Manager Selection Committee (4.9 GHz Committee) and providing herein the Commission-approved public interest determination. The 4.9 GHz Committee's objectives and scope of activities are to provide the Commission with advice and recommendations on the selection of a 4.9 GHz Band Manager to coordinate operations in the 4.9 GHz band (4940-4990 MHz) through optimizing public safety use, facilitating the integration of the latest commercially available technologies and benefitting public safety users. The 4.9 GHz Committee will receive and review proposals from persons or entities seeking to serve as Band Manager and to hold the Band Manager overlay license. The 4.9 GHz Committee will operate for no more than one year from the date of establishment unless the Commission directs that it terminate on an earlier date. A copy of the charter will be posted on the Agency's website at
www.fcc.gov.

The FCC envisioned in the Seventh R&O in WP Docket No. 07-100 (38 FCC Rcd at 712, para. 21) that the Band Manager would be recommended by a selection committee “that represents and ensures the involvement of the relevant stakeholders, in particular the public safety community.” The Commission in the Eighth R&O in WP Docket No. 07-100 (39 FCC Rcd at 12066, para. 52) also delegated “broad authority” to the Public Safety and Homeland Security and Wireless Telecommunications Bureaus “to establish the procedures by which a selection committee will be chosen, identify representatives to sit on the selection committee, determine the requisite number of selection committee members, identify the applicable selection criteria, and establish the appropriate procedures and appropriate oversight for the selection process as part of choosing the Band Manager.”

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, this notice announces that the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), will submit the collection of information abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and comment. The PRA submission describes the nature of the information collection and its expected cost and burden, and it includes the actual data collection instrument.
DATES:
Comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent by November 20, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To submit comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection, please type the following link into your browser:
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain,
select “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments”, then search the list for the information collection by Title or “OMB Control No. 2900-0770.”
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
VA PRA information: Dorothy Glasgow, 202-461-1084,
VAPRA@va.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Generic Clearance for the Collection of Qualitative Feedback on Agency Service Delivery (VBA, VHA, NCA).
Type of Review:
Revision of a currently approved collection.
Abstract:
Order 12862 directs Federal agencies to provide service to the public that matches or exceeds the best service available in the private sector. In order to work continuously to ensure that our programs are effective and meet our customers' needs, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) seeks to obtain OMB approval of a generic clearance to collect qualitative feedback on our service delivery for Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA); Veterans Health Administration (VHA); and National Cemetery Administration (NCA). By qualitative feedback, we mean information that provides useful insights on perceptions and opinions, but not statistical surveys that yield quantitative results that can be generalized to the population of study.
The proposed information collection activity provides a means to garner qualitative customer and stakeholder feedback in an efficient, timely manner, in accordance with the Administration's commitment to improving service delivery. This feedback will provide insights into customer or stakeholder perceptions, experiences and expectations, provide an early warning of issues with service, or focus attention on areas where communication, training, or changes in operations might improve delivery of products or services. These collections will allow for ongoing, collaborative, and actionable communications between the VA and its customers and stakeholders. They will also provide feedback to contribute directly to the improvement of program management.
The solicitation of feedback will target areas such as timeliness, appropriateness, accuracy of information, courtesy, efficiency of service delivery, and resolution of issues with service delivery. Responses will be assessed to plan and inform efforts to improve or maintain the quality of service offered to the public. If this information is not collected, vital feedback from customers and stakeholders on the provision of services will be unavailable to the Agency.
The Agency will only submit information collections for approval under this generic clearance if they meet the following conditions:
The collections are voluntary;
The collections are low-burden for respondents (based on considerations of total burden hours, total number of respondents, or burden-hours per respondent) and are low-cost for both the respondents and the Federal Government;
The collections are noncontroversial and do not raise issues of concern to other Federal agencies;
Any collection is targeted to the solicitation of opinions from respondents who have experience with the program or may have experience with the program in the near future;
Personally identifiable information (PII) is collected only to the extent necessary and is not retained;
Information gathered will be used only internally for general service improvement and program management purposes and is not intended for release outside of the agency;
Information gathered will not be used for the purpose of substantially informing influential policy decisions; and
Information gathered will yield qualitative information; the collections will not be designed or expected to yield statistically reliable results or used as though the results are generalizable to the population of study.
The types of collections that this generic clearance covers include, but are not limited to, Program Satisfaction Surveys; Focus Groups; Customer Comment Cards; Small Discussion Groups of customers, potential customers, delivery partners, or other stakeholders; Qualitative Customer Satisfaction Surveys, such as post-transaction surveys and opt-out web surveys; In-person Observation Testing, such as website or software usability tests; and Patient Surveys. As a general matter, information collections under this clearance will not result in any new system of records containing privacy information and will not ask questions of a sensitive nature, such as sexual behavior and attitudes, religious beliefs, and other matters that are commonly
( printed page 66624)
considered private. There is an overall decrease in the anticipated number of respondents and burden hours due to adjustments based on agency program data.

Individuals or Households; Businesses and Organizations; State, Local or Tribal Government.
